reason:
Third airing of an absence refuted in round 3 (nothing-a-guest-sees-ever-moves) and round 7 (the-guest-never-sees-anything-move). It brings no new evidence, is LESS accurate than the version it repeats, and its named fix is wrong about the code in three places and actively harmful in a fourth.

1) THE PROBLEM STATEMENT IS FACTUALLY WRONG AND UNDERCOUNTS. 'The whole product contains one moment of motion... and it lives inside the owner's editor, which the audience never opens' is false. b.css declares EIGHT transitions (lines 184, 357, 369, 401, 646, 768, 802), and driving state=phone and state=desk at 390x844 and 1440x960 the received DOM carries eight transition-bearing elements: seven copies of `top` on .b-item plus `.b-behindSummary` (a <summary>, 'Behind you / 3 moments') with `background var(--t-fast)`. That is a disclosure control the audience presses, with declared motion, in the received view. Round 7's version of this finding counted seven correctly; this one counts one. The zero-@keyframes and no-.animate() claims are true, but they were true and accepted in rounds 3 and 7.

2) THE FIX IS WRONG ABOUT THE CODE IT CLAIMS TO REUSE. (a) '--i, the row index already available at render' does not exist: `grep -- '--i' b.css render-b.js` returns nothing. (b) 'the existing prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference guard' does not exist. The only guard is `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` in shell.css:341-348, which is the opposite polarity. Two of the fix's three load-bearing hooks are invented.

3) IT BREAKS REDUCED MOTION, AND CITES THE BLIND GATE AS PROOF THAT IT DOES NOT. shell.css:341-348 clamps animation-duration, animation-iteration-count, transition-duration and scroll-behavior. It does NOT clamp animation-delay. With `both` fill and `animation-delay: calc(var(--i) * 60ms)`, the delays survive reduce untouched. I injected the proposal verbatim under emulateMedia({reducedMotion:'reduce'}) at 390x844 and sampled computed opacity: 0ms `0 0 0 0 0 0 0`; 99ms `1 1 0 0 0 0 0`; 191ms `1 1 1 1 0 0 0`; 285ms `1 1 1 1 1 0 0`; 380ms all seven. A reader who has asked the OS for no motion gets the entire plan blank at first paint and seven hard pop-ins over 380ms - jerkier than the animation, and strictly worse than the flat paint it replaces. The finding's assurance that 'the reduced-motion assertion keeps holding' is true and is the indictment: interaction-check.mjs:812-821 measures transitionDuration only, so the gate would pass green while the harm ships. audit.mjs:400-416 is equally blind - it reads transitionDuration and transitionTimingFunction, never animation-*.

4) IT VIOLATES THE DIRECTION'S WRITTEN MOTION DOCTRINE, WHICH IS THE EXACT TEST THE BRIEF SETS. b.css:181-184 verbatim: 'Position is the quantity in this direction, so animating position renders the change of the quantity rather than decorating a state change.' `b-rise` is `translateY(4px)` - animating position to decorate a state change, the one thing the doctrine names and forbids. `b-draw` scaleY on the rail animates a length that represents the plan's span, a quantity that is not changing at all. Neither earns its way past the doctrine; both are the decoration it was written to exclude. LANGUAGE.md:28 'motion answers something the reader did' and lock.md:101-103 'nothing floats idly' say the same. Opening a link is not an act on the measure.

5) IT IS OFF THE DECLARED LADDER, AND GETS THERE BY ABANDONING THE CAP RATHER THAN MEETING IT. Ladder is [0, 0.08, 0.14, 0.22] (elevate.config.json) with one easing. 60ms is on no ladder; a 600ms cap is on no ladder; a 7-step delay series 0/60/120/180/240/300/360ms is a second, undeclared ladder. Round 7 refuted the 0.08s-stagger version because seven rows cannot settle inside its own 0.3s cap using declared values; round 8's answer is to invent 60ms and double the cap. That is not new evidence, it is the same arithmetic failure with the constraint removed.

6) IT REGRESSES A ROUND-7 RATIFIED DECISION. .b-tick and .b-away are children of .b-item (verified in the driven DOM). A translateY(4px) on the row takes the tick 4px off the true pixel on the rail - for the last row, until 360ms. Round 7 ratified 'only the tick stays on the true pixel' and b.css:200-208 argues at length that the count and the words move as one object or they are not one object. The proposal breaks the tick off the rail during precisely the moment it is asking the reader to trust the rail.

7) MOST OF IT PLAYS WHERE NOBODY IS LOOKING. At 390x844, the flagship case, .b-rail measures 1034px tall in an 844px viewport. A scaleY(0)->scaleY(1) sweep and four of seven staggered rows finish below the fold. lessons.md:38 is explicit: 'play animations inside the visible area.'

The seat is honest that this is taste, and the observation of the absence is accurate. But the absence is the declared position, argued in writing at the point of the code, and has now been examined and upheld twice. The fix offered to replace it is unbuildable as written, off the ladder, contrary to the doctrine, and measurably harmful to reduced-motion readers.
sharpenedFix: None. If a future round revisits arrival at all, the only version that could survive: opacity alone, no transform, one 0.22s duration on --ease, no stagger and no per-row delay, applied to a single above-the-fold element in one state, gated on data-arrived, and shipped only alongside a NEW assertion in interaction-check.mjs that animation-delay and animation-duration both collapse under reduce - because the current assertion cannot see either. Anything with a delay series is off-ladder by construction.
